chunks: "A microcontroller has a few different kinds of memory on the same chip, and they're all mapped into one address space so the CPU reaches them with ordinary loads and stores.
Program code and constants live in flash, which is non-volatile, so the firmware survives power-off.
Working data, meaning variables, the stack and the heap, lives in SRAM, which is fast and writable but loses everything when power goes away. Then there are the registers.

The CPU's own core registers hold the values it is operating on right now, and the peripheral registers, like a GPIO output register or a timer compare value, are mapped at fixed addresses, so writing to that address actually changes hardware.

When I compile C, the linker sorts things out: code and const data go to flash, initialised globals get stored in flash and copied into RAM by the startup code, uninitialised globals are zeroed in RAM, and local variables go on the stack.
If I need data to survive power cycles, like calibration values or a serial number, I put it in EEPROM or a flash page that I write deliberately.
A typical small part might have 64 KB of flash and 20 KB of SRAM, so I always keep an eye on how much RAM the stack and heap take."
